assets/annotations/korean_honggildong_l1.title: 1. 아버지라고 부를 수 없는 아이
assets/annotations/korean_honggildong_l1.text:
옛날에 홍 판서라는 사람이 있었습니다. 홍 판서는 나라에서 높은 벼슬에 있었습니다. 나라에서 중요한 일을 했고, 많은 사람들이 그를 잘 알았습니다.

홍 판서에게는 두 아들이 있었습니다. 첫째 아들은 홍인형이었습니다. 인형의 어머니는 유 부인이었습니다. 유 부인은 홍 판서의 아내였습니다. 둘째 아들은 홍길동이었습니다. 길동의 어머니는 춘섬이었습니다.

춘섬은 처음에 홍 판서의 집에서 일하는 사람이었습니다. 나중에는 홍 판서와 함께 살게 되었습니다. 그리고 길동이 태어났습니다. 홍 판서는 아들을 보고 기분이 아주 좋았습니다. 하지만 길동의 어머니가 유 부인이 아니라서 마음이 아프기도 했습니다.

길동은 여덟 살이 되었습니다. 공부를 아주 잘했습니다. 하나를 배우면 다른 것도 많이 알 수 있었습니다. 홍 판서는 길동을 더 많이 사랑했습니다.

하지만 길동은 형과 똑같이 살 수 없었습니다. 춘섬은 집에서 일하는 사람이었고, 사람들은 춘섬을 중요한 사람으로 생각하지 않았습니다. 사람들은 춘섬의 아들인 길동도 중요한 사람으로 생각하지 않았습니다. 길동이 홍 판서를 ‘아버지’라고 부르면 홍 판서는 화를 냈습니다. 인형을 ‘형’이라고 불러도 화를 냈습니다.

길동은 이제 열 살보다 나이가 많았습니다. 하지만 아버지를 ‘아버지’라고 부를 수 없었습니다. 형을 ‘형’이라고 부를 수도 없었습니다. 그 집에서 일하는 다른 사람들도 길동을 중요한 사람으로 생각하지 않았습니다. 길동은 마음이 매우 아팠습니다.

어느 가을 밤이었습니다. 달이 밝았습니다. 길동은 책을 읽고 있었습니다. 그리고 더 읽지 않고 말했습니다.

“나는 나라를 돕고 큰 일을 하고 싶다. 그런데 왜 이렇게 혼자인 것 같을까? 나에게도 아버지가 있다. 형도 있다. 하지만 아버지를 아버지라고 부를 수 없다. 형을 형이라고 부를 수도 없다. 정말 마음이 아프다.”

길동은 집 밖으로 나갔습니다. 그리고 칼을 가지고 싸우는 연습을 했습니다. 홍 판서도 밖에서 달을 보고 있었습니다. 길동을 보고 불렀습니다.

“밤이 늦었는데 왜 아직 안 자니?”

길동은 대답했습니다.

“달이 좋아서 보고 있었습니다. 다른 사람들은 모두 중요한 사람입니다. 그런데 저는 그렇지 않습니다. 저도 사람인데, 왜 저는 다른 사람들과 다릅니까?”

홍 판서는 길동의 말을 이해했습니다. 그런데도 화를 내며 물었습니다.

“그게 무슨 말이냐?”

길동이 다시 말했습니다.

“저는 아버지의 아들입니다. 아버지와 어머니께 감사합니다. 하지만 저는 아버지를 ‘아버지’라고 부를 수 없습니다. 형을 ‘형’이라고 부를 수도 없습니다. 그래서 항상 슬픕니다.”

길동은 울었습니다. 홍 판서도 마음이 아팠습니다. 하지만 길동에게 좋은 말을 해 주면, 길동이 아버지의 말을 듣지 않을까 걱정했습니다. 그래서 길동에게 크게 화를 냈습니다.

“높은 벼슬을 하는 사람의 집에서 일하는 여자의 아들은 너만 있는 것이 아니다. 왜 너는 이런 말을 하느냐? 다시 이런 말을 하면 내 앞에 올 수 없다.”

길동은 아무 말도 할 수 없었습니다. 아버지 앞에서 계속 울었습니다.

“이제 돌아가라.”

홍 판서의 말을 듣고 길동은 방으로 돌아갔습니다. 방에서도 길동의 마음은 계속 슬펐습니다.

entries.explanation_en: After a time expression, 에 says when something happens.
Marks the noun that is the subject of a statement.
Sets up the noun that the rest of the statement is about; it can also signal contrast.
Connects a noun to another noun it owns or is related to.
Marks the noun affected by the verb.
Follows a name before a noun to say what that person or thing is called.
Marks the name or words used with a verb such as ‘call’ or ‘say’.
Places the action or state before now. The written form changes with the preceding stem.
Ends a statement in a formal, polite style.
Turns a descriptive word into a modifier placed before its noun.
After an action verb, this form describes a noun by an action already completed.
Forms a modifier for an action considered possible or expected; before 수 it helps express ability or possibility.
Connects a noun to what someone or something is. It can take past and polite endings.
A verb in its -(으)ㄹ modifier form followed by 수 없다 means that doing it is not possible.
Attach 에서 to a place noun to mark where an action takes place. The same form follows nouns ending in a consonant or a vowel.
Attach 도 to a noun to mean ‘also’ or ‘too’. With emphasis, it can mean ‘even’. It usually replaces a subject, topic, or object marker, but can follow other particles.

Attach -게 to a verb or descriptive stem and follow it with 하다. The construction means to make or let someone perform an action, or to cause a state. When the action is negative, it can express preventing someone from doing something.

Attach -고 to a verb or descriptive stem to connect it to another action or description, often meaning ‘and’. The final predicate can supply the tense for both connected parts when they share the same time.
Before 아니다, mark the noun naming what someone or something is not with 이 after a consonant or 가 after a vowel. This noun gives the identity or category being denied.
Attach -지 to a verb stem and follow it with 못하다 to express inability to perform the action. The inability may come from lack of skill or from circumstances that prevent the action.

Attach -는 to an action verb stem and place the resulting modifier before a noun. Drop a stem-final ㄹ before adding -는. The modifier describes an ongoing or habitual action associated with the noun. Its time is understood relative to the main statement, so it can describe an action taking place at a past time.

A verb modifier followed by 수 있다 expresses ability or possibility. Add -을 to a stem ending in a consonant other than ㄹ, or -ㄹ to a vowel-ending stem; a ㄹ-ending stem keeps its ㄹ. Follow this modifier with 수 있다 to mean ‘can do’.

Attach -기도 하다 to an action or descriptive stem to add another action or state, meaning ‘also do’ or ‘also be’. The predicate becomes a noun-like expression with -기, 도 adds ‘also’, and 하다 completes the predicate.

Attach -게 to a descriptive stem to describe how an action happens or the degree of a quality. With an action verb, -게 can link the action to a following predicate that controls or changes whether it happens.

Place a clause in noun-modifying form before 것 같다 to express an impression or an uncertain judgment: ‘seems’ or ‘appears’. For a current description, use -(으)ㄴ with descriptive predicates or -인 after a noun; for an ongoing action, use -는 with an action verb.
Before 되다, attach 이 to a consonant-ending noun or 가 to a vowel-ending noun. This marked noun identifies the role, state, or age that someone or something reaches.

Connect an action verb to 주다 with -아/어 to present the action as done for someone. Use -아 when the stem's final vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ and -어 otherwise; 하다 becomes 해. The person receiving the benefit may be stated or understood.

Attach -게 되다 to an action verb stem to describe a change in circumstances or a resulting situation, often meaning ‘come to do’ or ‘end up doing’. The construction emphasizes how the situation develops rather than a deliberate decision.

Attach 으로 after a consonant other than ㄹ, or 로 after a vowel or ㄹ. With predicates of judgment or classification, the marked noun gives the role or category in which someone or something is regarded: ‘as’.

Attach 보다 to the noun or quantity used as the comparison point. The following predicate states how something differs from it. 보다 has the same form after consonants and vowels; 더 may be added to emphasize ‘more’.
With predicates of sameness or difference, attach 와 after a vowel or 과 after a consonant to mark the comparison partner. English may use ‘the same as’ or ‘different from’, depending on the predicate.

Attach -아도 or -어도 to an action or descriptive stem to say that the following result holds despite that condition: ‘even if’ or ‘even though’. Use -아도 after a stem whose final vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ and -어도 otherwise; 하다 becomes 해도. Regular contractions and irregular stem changes apply.

Attach -으면 after a stem ending in a consonant other than ㄹ, or -면 after a vowel or ㄹ. This introduces a condition, meaning ‘if’, or a regularly occurring situation, meaning ‘when’. For nouns, use -이면 after a consonant or -면 after a vowel.

entries.title_en: Linking a verb to an auxiliary
entries.explanation_en: The -아/어 form connects a verb to a following auxiliary that adds meaning to the action. Use -아 when the stem's final vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ and -어 otherwise; 하다 becomes 해. Vowels may contract, and irregular verbs may change their stems. The following auxiliary determines the meaning of the complete construction.

This connective supplies background for the next clause or introduces a contrast. Use -는데 with action verbs and 있다 or 없다. With descriptive stems, use -은데 after a consonant or -ㄴ데 after a vowel; drop a final ㄹ before -ㄴ데. Use -인데 after nouns and -는데 after a past-marked stem.

Attach -으며 after a stem ending in a consonant other than ㄹ, or -며 after a vowel or ㄹ. It connects simultaneous actions or joins related actions and descriptions, meaning ‘while’ or ‘and’. It is especially common in written language.

Attach -인 to a noun to make it identify or classify a following noun. This is the noun-modifying form of 이다 and means ‘who is’ or ‘which is’. The form -인 follows both consonant-ending and vowel-ending nouns.
Attach -고 싶다 to an action verb stem to mean ‘want to do’. It normally expresses the speaker's own desire in a statement or asks about the listener's desire in a question.
Attach 으로 after a consonant other than ㄹ, or 로 after a vowel or ㄹ, to indicate the direction or destination of movement. It presents the place as where someone or something heads.
Attach 만 to a noun to restrict a statement to that person, thing, or quantity: ‘only’. It has the same form after consonants and vowels and can follow some other particles.

entries.title_en: Existing or present before a noun
entries.explanation_en: Use 있는 before a noun to describe something that exists, is present, or is available, and 없는 for something absent or unavailable. 있다 and 없다 take -는 in this use, giving 있는 and 없는.
Attach -습니까 to a consonant-ending predicate stem or -ㅂ니까 to a vowel-ending stem to ask a formal polite question. Drop a stem-final ㄹ before adding -ㅂ니까. With a noun, use -입니까.

Attach 께 to a noun referring to a respected person to mark the recipient or person toward whom an action is directed. It is the respectful counterpart of 에게 and has the same form after consonants and vowels.

Attach -아라 to an action stem whose final vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ and -어라 otherwise to give a plain command. 하다 becomes 해라, and adjoining vowels may contract. This direct style is used with someone younger or lower in status, or in familiar speech.
Attach -니 to a predicate stem to ask a familiar, non-polite question, usually to someone close or younger. Drop a stem-final ㄹ before -니. After a noun, use -이니 after a consonant or -니 after a vowel.

Attach 에 to a place noun to mark where someone or something is, or the destination of movement. It has the same form after consonants and vowels. Use 에서 instead when marking the place where an action takes place.

Attach -지 directly to an action or descriptive stem before a negative auxiliary such as 않다. The -지 form links the predicate to the auxiliary; the auxiliary supplies the negation and completes the construction.
Attach -지 않다 to an action or descriptive stem to negate its meaning: ‘do not’ or ‘be not’. The original predicate takes -지, while 않다 completes the negative predicate.

Put a clause in noun-modifying form before 것이 아니다 to mean ‘it is not the case that’. Use -는 for an ongoing action or 있다 and 없다, -(으)ㄴ for a current description, or -인 after a noun. 것 turns the clause into a situation that 아니다 denies; the wording determines which part of the claim is rejected.

entries.title_en: Turning an action or state into a noun
entries.explanation_en: Attach -기 to an action or descriptive stem to make a noun-like expression referring to doing something or being in a state. It can take particles or appear within a larger grammatical construction.
Attach 와 after a vowel-ending noun or 과 after a consonant-ending noun to join it to another noun, meaning ‘and’. A particle attached to the final noun can apply to the coordinated group.

Plain statements are common in narration, private thoughts, and non-polite speech. Descriptive predicates and 있다 or 없다 take -다. Present action verbs take -ㄴ다 after a vowel or -는다 after a consonant; drop a final ㄹ before -ㄴ다. A noun takes -이다, and a past-marked predicate takes -다.

These endings ask direct questions in a non-polite style. -냐 can follow a predicate stem. The fuller forms are -느냐 with action verbs and 있다 or 없다, and -(으)냐 with descriptive predicates. Drop a stem-final ㄹ before these endings. Nouns take -이냐 after a consonant or -냐 after a vowel. The style may sound familiar or stern depending on the relationship and tone.
Attach 들 to a noun to make its plural meaning explicit, especially with people. Korean nouns can also have plural meaning without 들, so this marker is not required whenever English uses a plural.

Attach 에 to a noun naming a position, role, or state to mark what someone or something occupies or is in. With 있다, this can express holding a position or being in a particular state. The same form follows consonants and vowels.

With 있다 or 없다, attach 에게 to the person who has or lacks something. The possessed thing or relationship is normally marked with 이 or 가. This structure often translates into English with ‘have’ rather than ‘there is’.
Attach -고 있다 to an action verb stem to describe an action in progress, often translated as ‘be doing’. 있다 functions as an auxiliary here, rather than independently stating that something exists.

Attach -아서 to a stem whose final vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ and -어서 otherwise to give a reason for the following statement. 하다 becomes 해서, and 아니다 becomes 아니라서. Regular contractions and irregular stem changes apply. The final predicate normally establishes the time of the whole statement.

entries.title_en: The person an action is directed to
entries.explanation_en: Attach 에게 to a person or animal to mark the recipient or the one toward whom an action is directed, often translated as ‘to’. It has the same form after consonants and vowels.

Use -(으)ㄹ까 to ask a question inwardly or wonder about an explanation or possibility. Add -을까 after a consonant other than ㄹ, or -ㄹ까 after a vowel; a ㄹ-ending stem takes -까. Nouns take -일까. The ending conveys reflection or uncertainty rather than necessarily referring to future time.
Place 안 before an action or descriptive predicate to negate it. With many activity nouns followed by 하다, 안 goes between the noun and 하다. To deny a noun identity, use 아니다 instead.

Use -(으)ㄹ까 to consider whether something might happen or be true. Add -을까 after a consonant other than ㄹ, or -ㄹ까 after a vowel; a ㄹ-ending stem takes -까. Nouns take -일까. Before a predicate of worry, the clause identifies the uncertain possibility causing concern.
Attach 와 after a vowel-ending noun or 과 after a consonant-ending noun to mark a companion or someone participating in an action together: ‘with’. 함께 or 같이 may follow to emphasize doing it together.
